Patients with all forms of blepharitis can benefit from eyelid hygiene (eg, warm compresses, scrubbing eyelid margins with baby shampoo or tea tree oil). C

background.definition: Blepharitis is a chronic inflammation of the eyelid margins with redness, thickening, formation of scales and crust or shallow marginal ulcers. Blepharitis can be divided anatomically into anterior blepharitis (involving eyelashes and follicles) and posterior blepharitis (involving dysfunction of the meibomian glands). See .

list.listitem: Blepharitis is one of the most common ocular disorders. Ophthalmologists and optometrists report that blepharitis affects approximately one-third of their patients.

Anterior blepharitis is mainly centered on the eyelashes and follicles and can be associated with seborrhea, Demodex infestation (D. folliculorum) or infection with staphylococci, streptococcus pyogenes or pseudomonas aeruginosa.

Posterior blepharitis is due to dysfunction of the meibomian glands. Other important associations include acne rosacea, herpes simplex virus, dermatitis, varicella-zoster dermatitis, Demodex infestation (D. brevis), and allergic/contact dermatitis.
Eyelash extensions can cause allergic blepharitis from glues and eyelid-fixing tapes.

The pathophysiology of blepharitis often involves staphylococcal colonization or Demodex infestation of the eyelids. Bacterial enzymes, toxins, and waste products invade the eyelid tissue and create a damaging cell-mediated immune reaction. Increased colonization is seen if the patient has seborrheic dermatitis or meibomian gland dysfunction.
Suspect blepharitis in patients with recurrent itchy eyes and eyelid irritation.

In addition to history and external exam, slit lamp examination can distinguish between anterior blepharitis (loss of eyelashes, matted eyelid deposits) and posterior blepharitis (oily eyelid deposits, chalazia).
Consider cultures and suspect Demodex infestation in patients with recurrent symptoms and in those who are treatment resistant.

Differential.Differential_Features: Erythema of the eye (rather than eyelids)
Red tender bump in eyelid, acute infection of an oil gland of eyelid
Firm nontender bump, chronic sterile inflammation of an oil gland of eyelid
Telangiectasia, papules, pustules, rhinophyma, and prominent sebaceous glands
Comedones, erythema with occasional cystic lesions
Hyperpigmentation, fine scaling with less edema
Persistent eyelid findings, insidious onset, and typically painless nodules

list.listitem: Patients typically present with itching, burning and redness of the eyelid margins. They can also present with lid irritation, edema and loss or misdirection of lashes (particularly with Staph infection). Soft, oily, yellow scaling around the lashes distinguishes blepharitis from other causes of eyelid inflammation.

Other common complaints include dry or watery eyes, foreign body sensation, increased frequency of blinking, crusting of the lashes with medial canthus erythema, red eye, photophobia and contact lens intolerance., Ulcerations may be seen in severe cases. Symptoms are usually worse in the morning (if symptoms are worse at night, suspect aqueous deficient dry eye).

Demodex infestation is present in at least 30% and up to 70% of patients with chronic blepharitis, increasing with age., Prevalence in asymptomatic patients is similar, but patients with lack of response to other therapies often improve with Demodex eradication.

The physical examination should include assessment of visual acuity and external examination of the skin and eyelids. Seborrhea dermatitis of the scalp, brows and ears is frequently associated with the seborrheic form of blepharitis.
summarizes the characteristics of anterior and posterior blepharitis. D. folliculorum is commonly associated with anterior and D. brevis with posterior blepharitis.

The definitive diagnosis is made by slit lamp examination to assess the tear film, anterior eyelid margin, eyelashes, posterior eyelid margin, tarsal conjunctiva, bulbar conjunctiva and cornea (see ).
Suspect eyelid carcinoma in patients with marked asymmetry, resistance to therapy, or unifocal recurrent chalazia that do not respond well to therapy.
There are no diagnostic tests to confirm suspected blepharitis.

Patients with recurrent or severe symptoms and those who do not respond to treatment should have a culture of the eyelid secretions. Presence of collarettes at the base of the eyelid follicle on slit lamp or lash epilation with mite counts on microscopy can diagnose Demodex infestation.
Digital photographic images can be useful in the hands of ophthalmologists for grading signs of anterior blepharitis.
Biopsy of the eyelid may be indicated to exclude carcinoma when there is marked asymmetry or resistance to therapy.
Suspect blepharitis in patients with recurrent itchy eyes and lid irritation.
Start with conservative measures such as warm compresses, lid scrubs with baby shampoo, and topical antibiotics.
Refer patients with suspected blepharitis for a slit lamp examination if they do not respond to conservative measures.
When patients fail treatment, consider Demodex mite infestation or ocular rosacea.,

Patients with all forms of blepharitis can benefit from eyelid hygiene (eg, warm compresses, scrubbing eyelid margins with a cotton swab dipped in baby shampoo, lid wipes with tea tree oil) for symptomatic relief. Once-or twice-daily compresses and massage, at a time most convenient for the patient, is generally adequate. B
Since anterior blepharitis is often staphylococcal, apply topical antibiotics such as bacitracin and erythromycin; these provide symptomatic relief and decrease bacteria from the eyelid margin. B

Since posterior blepharitis is often associated with chalazia or deeper infections, systemic azithromycin (500 mg followed by 250 mg for 4 days) or doxycycline (100 mg twice daily) should be used; data on efficacy in chronic blepharitis, however, are inconclusive. C
Demodicosis should be considered in patients who do not improve using the above treatments; treatment with 5% to 50% tea tree oil or Lotilaner topical solution can be considered. B
Refer patients with symptoms refractory to treatment, and refer patients with marked eyelid asymmetry, resistance to therapy, or unifocal recurrent chalazia to rule out carcinoma.
There is insufficient evidence to make definitive recommendations for the treatment of blepharitis and most treatments are consensus based.

Patients with blepharitis should be treated conservatively: warm compresses, eyelid scrubs or wipes with baby shampoo or tea tree oil, and topical antibiotics. Authors of a Cochrane review of 34 small trials of chronic blepharitis concluded that lid hygiene provides symptomatic relief.

Patients with anterior blepharitis, which is often staphylococcal in origin, should be treated with topical antibiotics. Options include bacitracin, erythromycin 0.5%, and azithromycin 1% 1-4 times daily for up to 14 days. In the Cochrane review cited above, topical antibiotics provide both symptomatic relief and eyelid margin bacterial eradication.

In a multicenter RCT of 122 patients, those with moderate-to-severe blepharitis/blepharoconjunctivitis randomized to tobramycin/dexamethasone (1 drop four times daily for 14 days) had greater improvement at day 8 (mean global score) than patients receiving azithromycin (1 drop twice daily for 2 days followed by once-daily dosing for 12 days).
Another small RCT showed that topical 1% azithromycin plus 0.1% dexamethasone may be more effective than azithromycin alone for resolving symptoms, but not more effective than dexamethasone alone.

Topical corticosteroid eye drops or ointments (or antibiotics/steroid combinations) may help control acute exacerbations of blepharitis, but long-term use is not recommended due to risk of developing increased intraocular pressure and cataract formation. Topical glucocorticoids should be prescribed by or in consultation with an ophthalmologist.

For patients with meibomian gland dysfunction (posterior blepharitis), small studies demonstrate that oral azithromycin (500 mg day 1, 250 mg day 2-5) yields better outcomes than tetracyclines, and is preferred for women of childbearing age and children. Overall, data on usefulness of systemic antibiotics for chronic blepharitis are inconclusive.

Blepharitis associated with Demodex species infestation can be treated with 5% to 50% tea tree oil (see below), but clinical effectiveness is unclear. Topical ivermectin may benefit some cases of recalcitrant Demodex blepharitis.

Multiple studies including 4 RCT's recently demonstrated that lotilaner ophthalmic solution 0.25% 1 drop twice daily (lotilaner is an ectoparasiticide) is effective in Demodex mite eradication with minimal side effects, and it received FDA approval in 2023.
There may be a role for topical cyclosporin in patients with posterior blepharitis.

Tea tree oil 50% eyelid scrub treatment was effective in one RCT for eliminating ocular Demodex and improving ocular symptoms. However, authors of a Cochrane review of 6 RCTs concluded that there was uncertainty about the effectiveness of tea tree oil (5% to 50%) for short-term treatment of Demodex blepharitis but that if using this treatment, consider a lower dose to avoid ocular irritation.

In a recent trial of in-office Microblepharoexfoliation treatment followed by terpinen-4-ol lid scrubs (the main component of tea tree oil) or sham scrubs twice daily for 1 month in 50 patients with Demodex positive blepharitis, infestation levels were reduced but there was no clear effect on clinical improvement.
Small RCT's show that both terpinen-4-ol wipes and tea tree oil swabs reduce blepharitis symptoms more than baby shampoo.
In-office intense pulsed light (IPL) also has variable response and limitations with darker skin tones (Fitzpatrick V or VI).
Artificial tears may improve symptoms when used as an adjunct to eyelid cleansing and medications.
Apply warm compresses on a daily basis for several minutes to loosen crusting, followed by brief gentle massage of the eyelid to express meibomian secretions.
All forms of blepharitis should be treated with eyelid hygiene consisting of wipes, swabs or baby shampoo.
Refer patients with symptoms refractory to treatment.
Refer patients with marked eyelid asymmetry, resistance to therapy or unifocal recurrent chalazia to rule out carcinoma.
Refer patients with severe eye redness, pain, light sensitivity, impaired vision or corneal abnormalities.
Educate the patient about the chronicity and recurrence of the eyelid symptoms, which can be controlled but rarely eliminated. C
Blepharitis is a chronic condition that has periods of exacerbation and remission. C
Severe staphylococcal blepharitis may eventually lead to eyelash loss, eyelid scarring with trichiasis (ingrowth or introversion of the eyelashes), and corneal scarring and neovascularization.

Patients with blepharitis appear to be at higher risk of anxiety and depression (hazard ratios 1.58 and 1.42, respectively), with 23% constantly worrying about their eyes and 47% experiencing difficulty driving at night.

Almost 40% of children with blepharitis symptoms present with the onset of blepharokeratoconjunctivitis (BKC), that can involve the cornea and varies from superficial punctate keratitis to perforation. Referral to ophthalmology is appropriate.

feature.caption: Typical Signs and Symptoms of Anterior and Posterior Blepharitis.
feature.feature_body: Anterior blepharitis (staphylococcal) Loss of eyelashes Matted, eyelid deposits Conjunctival injection Tear deficiency Corneal epithelial erosions (inferior, punctate) Frequent trichiasis (misdirection of eyelashes) Eyelid scarring Anterior blepharitis (seborrheic) Oily or greasy eyelid scaling Mild conjunctival injection Tear deficiency Corneal epithelial erosions (inferior, punctate) Associated with seborrheic dermatitis Posterior blepharitis (meibomian gland dysfunction) Excessive oily or greasy eyelid deposits Frequent chalazion formation Conjunctival injection Tear deficiency Corneal epithelial erosions (inferior, punctate) Association with rosacea Long-term complications include eyelid scarring and trichiasis
